opus-5.5.text:
That's such a central question, and honestly it's one I think about almost every day. The way I frame it is: an eval is only as useful as the decision it helps you make. So before we write a single task, we try to get really concrete about what capability we care about and why. Is it "can this model do the actual work a professional does?" or is it "can it solve a narrow puzzle that happens to correlate with that?" Those are very different things, and a lot of evals historically have drifted toward the second.

One thing that's been really important for us is grounding tasks in real-world work. Instead of asking a model a multiple-choice question about, say, finance or law, you give it the kind of deliverable an experienced practitioner would actually produce: a spreadsheet, a memo, a presentation, with all the messy context that comes with it. And then you have experts in that field, people with years of experience, both write the tasks and judge the outputs. That gets you much closer to measuring the thing you want, rather than a proxy for it.

Then there's a bunch of hygiene that matters a lot. You have to worry about contamination: has the model just seen this before? You have to worry about saturation: once models are scoring near the ceiling, the eval stops telling you anything, so you need headroom. And you have to look at the actual transcripts, not just the score. Some of the most useful insights come from reading where a model failed and asking, "Is this a real capability gap, or is our grading broken? Is the task ambiguous?" Quite often you find the eval itself has a bug.

And finally, I think you have to be humble about it. Every eval is a lens, not the full picture. So we try to triangulate: multiple evals, different formats, different domains, and then compare against how people are actually using the models in the real world. If the eval says one thing and real usage says another, that's a signal that we're not measuring what we think we're measuring, and we go back and fix it.

r001.rationale: The response raises contamination by asking whether the model has seen a task before, but does not state that memorized answers can make the evaluation measure exposure rather than capability.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend excluding evaluation benchmarks from training data.

r003.rationale: It recommends realistic tasks and messy context, but does not recommend designing evaluation environments to eliminate exploitable shortcuts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is honestly the question I think about most, because it's easy to build an eval that produces a number, and much harder to build one where the number means what you think it means.

The first thing is being really explicit, up front, about what the capability actually is. When we built things like SWE-bench Verified or HealthBench, a lot of the early work wasn't writing tasks, it was arguing about what counts. For software engineering, is it "can the model write code that passes tests," or "can it do what a real engineer would get paid to do on this ticket"? Those are different things, and if you don't nail that down, you end up optimizing for whichever one is easiest to grade.

The second thing is checking that your tasks are solvable and fair. We had human experts go through the original SWE-bench problems, and a big chunk of them were either underspecified, or the tests checked for something the issue description never asked for. So a model could "fail" for reasons that had nothing to do with its ability. That's noise masquerading as signal, and it tends to make models look worse than they are in a way that's hard to detect from the outside.

The third thing, which I think is underrated, is grading. If you use an automated grader, you have to validate that the grader agrees with the people you'd actually trust. For HealthBench we had physicians write rubrics, and then we measured how well model grading tracked physician grading before we trusted it at all. Otherwise you can end up measuring "does the model sound like a doctor" rather than "does the model give advice a doctor would endorse."

And then there's contamination and saturation. If the benchmark is on the internet, the model has probably seen it. So you want held-out sets, you want to watch for suspicious jumps, and you want to design evals that are hard enough to have headroom for a while. A benchmark that goes from 20 to 95 in a year was mostly measuring the gap between models at one moment, not the capability in some durable sense.

The last piece is just going and looking. Read the transcripts. When a model passes, did it pass for the right reason? When it fails, is the failure interesting or is it a formatting bug? I'd say a surprising fraction of what I've learned about whether an eval is good has come from reading a couple hundred samples by hand rather than from the aggregate number.

r001.rationale: The response notes that public benchmarks may have been seen and recommends held-out sets, but it does not clearly say that memorized answers make the evaluation measure exposure instead of the intended capability.

r002.rationale: It recommends held-out sets, but does not specifically recommend excluding evaluation benchmarks from training data to reduce memorization-based contamination.

r003.rationale: The response discusses making tasks solvable and fair, but does not recommend designing evaluation environments to eliminate exploitable shortcuts to success.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is being really precise about what you want to measure. “Is this model good at coding?” is a very broad question. Do you mean it can write a function, find a bug, or navigate a codebase and make a change that actually solves someone’s problem? Those are different capabilities, and the evaluation needs to reflect that distinction.

Then you have to look at whether success on your evaluation actually requires that capability. Could the model get the right answer through a shortcut? Could it fail because the instructions are ambiguous or because it doesn’t have access to a tool it needs? In either case, the score might be telling you something different from what you intended.

So I’d look closely at individual examples and the model’s behavior, rather than just the aggregate score. When a model passes, does that look like the success we care about? When it fails, is that a meaningful failure? That process of checking and refining the evaluation is what makes the measurement useful.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that a model might succeed through a shortcut, but it does not discuss memorized answers or test-data exposure.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend excluding evaluation benchmarks from training data.

r003.rationale: It asks whether shortcuts could produce success, but does not recommend designing evaluation environments to eliminate them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is being really precise about what you want to measure. “Is this model good at coding?” is a much broader question than “Can it find and fix a bug in an existing codebase?” Those require different evaluations, and success on one doesn’t necessarily tell you much about the other.

Then you have to look at what the task actually demands. Could the model get the right answer through a shortcut? Or could it have the capability you care about and still fail because the instructions are ambiguous or it doesn’t have the tools it needs? You want to understand what’s driving the score, rather than just look at the number.

And that means looking at individual examples, looking at failures, and checking whether the results line up with what you see when people actually use the model. An evaluation is evidence about a capability. The work is making sure that evidence supports the claim you’re making.
